extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of the history of advertising; historians of early modern trade and print
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and observed practices for producing, submitting, formatting, distributing, and editing newspaper advertisements in late 17th-century English periodicals (as recorded in a history/prospectus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution strategy / free circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should distribute copies widely and freely to booksellers, shops, inns, and principal coffee-houses and send them to most cities and principal towns in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example wording: 'He gives away every Monday above a thousand of them to all the Booksellers, shops and inns, and most of the principal coffee-houses in London and Westminster. Besides they are now sent to most of the cities and principal towns in England.' Purpose: increase reach and readership of advertisements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission process and insertion at reasonable rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person with matter to insert (titles of books, houses or land to be let or sold, persons removing, things lost, physicians' advertisements, inquiries for servants, etc.) may bring or send them to the Publisher who will carefully insert them at reasonable rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prospectus identifies a single office/publisher address (e.g., Tho. Howkins in George Yard, Lombard Street) as the place to submit copy and pay for insertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness vs. street bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing a weekly sheet of advertisements in a periodical is more advantageous and cheaper than handing out bills in the street.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prospectus claims one paper may be read twenty times while a bill is read once, and that the newspaper method can be done for at least the twentieth part of the charge and with greater success—use this for cost/ROI arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular publication schedule and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The advertisement sheet should appear on a regular, stated day (e.g., every week on Thursday morning) and be timed/placed where readers expecting civic information collect publications (e.g., where the Bills of Mortality are received).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit schedule increases usefulness to trade: 'shall come out every week on Thursday morning, and be delivered and dispersed in every house where the Bills of Mortality are received.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted content categories (comprehensive prospectus list)
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide range of commercial and public notices are appropriate: goods/merchandizes/ships for sale, ships to be let to freight and departure times, ships' names and burthens and inventories, parcels/materials for shipping, houses to let/sell/mortgage with notes of contents, lands for sale/mortgage, stage-coach erection/alteration/removal, advertisements of bargains, curious inventions/experiments for public view or sale, bankruptcy commissions, creditor notices, settlement or removal of public offices, schools and academies, baths/hot-houses, waterside keys and hoy arrivals, and similar lawful business notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prospectus lists these categories verbatim—useful as a template for what to accept/advertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office accessibility and customer service hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a fixed office open to receive advertisements and answer inquiries, with stated hours and location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The Office ... is kept in St Michael's Alley in Cornhilp London ... constant attendance every day in the Week shall be given, from Nine in the Morning, to Five in the Evening, to receive the desires of all Persons in matters of this nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy verification and opportunity to correct errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should invite masters/owners to inspect records to correct mistakes in dates and rates so books may be declared perfect at no charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prospectus asks owners to 'repair ... to the Office ... to see if no mistakes be in their several dales and rates, that the said Books may be declared perfect, which shall be no charge to the Persons concerned.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness due to limited space
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements must be concise because early papers were very small (folio half-sheets) and space limited; many ads ran in a single unbroken string.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes: 'Conciseness was of course necessary ... the paper was only a folio half-sheet' and many early notices appeared without breaks or full stops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and visual differentiation (later development)
rubrics_metrics.description: To attract attention among many ads publishers eventually used different types, dividing lines, woodcuts and other contrivances to distinguish notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although 'different types, dividing lines, woodcuts, and other contrivances' were at first unknown, the text recommends these as later solutions for standing out among competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative/political uses of the advertisement form
rubrics_metrics.description: The advertisement form can be used to expose sentiments, publish political satire or veiled messages—not only commercial content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from periodicals show satirical 'advertisements' (e.g., selling 'ships or castles in the air' or 'sedition seeds') used to comment on public grievances or political issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial recommendation and testimonial as credibility signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors frequently give personal testimony or character references for advertisers (e.g., 'I know a very eminent brewer' or 'from a valuable divine, my good friend, I have a very good character of him').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such first-person endorsements and cautious qualifying phrases ('I believe', 'I am informed') were used to signal respectability and to limit editorial liability—useful model for credibility-building in ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and preservation for long-term utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should plan for permanence by compiling volumes and indexes, including an index of all advertisements to make them useful for future reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prospectus: 'It's also lasting to be put into Volumes with indexes, and particularly there shall be an index of all the advertisements, whereby, for ages to come, they may be useful.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of addresses/places of abode to increase usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Listing addresses or places of abode for importers/advertisers significantly increases the practical value of advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Houghton added places of abode and a list of residences (doctors, shops) after being asked—'If desired I'll set down the places of abode ... I am often asked it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting by trade and profession
rubrics_metrics.description: Use trade- and profession-specific notices and tailor distribution to reach relevant audiences (barbers, clergy, schoolmasters, brokers, coaches, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The periodical explicitly targeted many trades and prepared lists (physicians, counsellors, attorneys, surgeons, gardeners, brokers, coaches and carriers) to serve specific commercial communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial gatekeeping and rejection of unsuitable copy
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor should exercise selectivity—reject duplicate or inappropriate notices and caution readers about quack remedies or poor solicitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I desire all booksellers to send me no new titles to old books, for they will be rejected.' and the editor's ironic 'Like lawyers, I take all causes. Who likes not may stop here.' show active editorial moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of urgency/time-sensitive phrasing in offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers should include urgency or timing information when relevant (e.g., seasonal opportunities, next malting time) to motivate prompt action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example ad: 'only thus much I must advise, if provision be not made speedily, the opportunity will be lost for the next malting time.' Use explicit time cues to prompt response.
